Threat.value: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard

issues.item: Expressions of Affection: Physical affection such as hugs
issues.explanation: These trigger items are not clinically coherent with the indexed trauma of mugging/robbery. Physical affection such as hugs is difficult to connect to robbery-related threat activation without any supporting appraisal, memory, or strategy content, and it conflicts with the otherwise stranger/sudden-movement threat profile. Crash imagery is more characteristic of road traffic trauma than robbery and lacks any plausible link to the reported threat items.

issues.item: Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
issues.explanation: The trigger item about cars being hit in an accident is hard to reconcile with the validated trauma type of mugging/robbery. The other trigger and threat items coherently suggest interpersonal danger and hypervigilance around strangers/crowding, but crash imagery points to a motor vehicle trauma theme that is not reflected elsewhere in the profile or in the cognitive formulation. This is more than unusual; it appears to reference a different trauma context.

vignette:
Rajesh, a 76-year-old South Asian electrician living in Queens, had always prided himself on being steady and self-sufficient. That changed one cold November evening when he was leaving a commercial building after finishing a late wiring job. The street was still busy with people heading home, and as he turned into a narrow alley toward his van, a man lurched out from behind a dumpster—reeking of cheap whiskey—shoved him against the wall, and ripped the heavy tool bag from his shoulder. Rajesh fell hard on the pavement, the smell of alcohol burning in his nostrils as the man vanished into the crowd. He drove home in a daze, shaken but not seriously injured, and told his wife it was nothing more than a fright.

In the weeks that followed, the incident stayed with him in ways he hadn’t expected. He began waking in the middle of the night, breath quick and heart pounding, the dream already dissolving but the feeling of being helpless and blind-sided lingering like a residue. Those nighttime hours became unbearable—he found it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, lying awake listening to every creak of the house, convinced that darkness offered cover for anyone who might harm him. The moment his eyes opened from a nightmare, he was already scanning the shadows, his mind racing with who could be there.

Out in the world, the same vigilance took hold. Rajesh had worked as an electrician for over forty years, often in crowded job sites or walking through busy streets to reach supply shops. Now, crowds felt different. People pressing close to him on the sidewalk or jostling at a hardware store checkout made his shoulders tense. He began to feel threatened by strangers approaching him even in ordinary situations—a man asking for directions, a delivery driver walking too quickly his way. Any sudden movement by another person put him immediately on guard; he would stop mid-stride, hands balling into fists, waiting for the shove, the grab. The smell of alcohol, even from someone just walking past a bar or a broken bottle on the curb, could snap him back to that alley in an instant. He would turn and walk the other way, heart hammering, certain that the person was about to close in.

These reactions built into a daily cycle. A glimpse of a crowded subway platform triggered a wave of threat that made him feel unsafe among strangers; the threat, in turn, made him hyperalert to every abrupt shift in body language, every unexpected advance. The more he stayed watchful, the more triggers seemed to jump out at him. He started leaving for work earlier to avoid rush hours and began taking longer, quieter routes, even though they tired him out. His wife noticed he no longer joined her for evening walks in the neighborhood, and his supervisor commented that he seemed jumpy around the other electricians on site. Rajesh knew he was overreacting, but the sense of danger felt real—too real to ignore.

What finally brought him to seek help was a moment in his own kitchen. His grandson, visiting for the weekend, ran toward him with a sudden excited dash—and Rajesh flinched so violently he knocked over a chair, frightening the boy. That evening, his wife said quietly, “You can’t go on like this.” Rajesh agreed, though he had no idea what talking about it would change. He still dreaded the dark, still felt his pulse spike when a stranger appeared too close, and the smell of alcohol remained an instant alarm. He came to the clinic hoping for a way to feel steady again in his own life, without having to scan every crowd and every shadow. What scared him most was the thought that this watchfulness would never lift—that he would spend his remaining years trapped inside his own alertness, jumped by a memory every time someone moved too fast.
